source.title: A Systematic Study of Behavioral Cloning for Scientific Data Annotation

record.tranche_reason: The study extends scaling and downstream-performance questions to multi-task behavioral-cloning models for scientific annotation, a different training regime from language-model pretraining.
record.gate_note: The paper reports scaling-related results for behavioral-cloning training loss and downstream task metrics. It does not fit or report power-law exponents, and its loss curves are training loss rather than held-out pretraining loss. Results cited from other studies are not included as rows.
record.test_reason: The study trains four sizes (25M–320M) of multi-task behavioral-cloning vision-language models and reports loss against tokens and FLOPs, plus downstream task metrics by size. This is a new training regime with results bearing on V5 and V6. It fits no power law, so the V5 evidence is directional only.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. Add that the authors quantify the data-efficiency gain (about 3× per 10× parameters) and call it consistent with LM scaling laws. Also add that at equal loss smaller models make better decisions, and that placement precision shows inverse scaling. The main text and the Fig 22 caption disagree on which size has lower loss at equal FLOPs.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains vision-language behavioral-cloning models on synthetic scientific-annotation tasks and examines training loss against tokens and compute; it does not use the original language-model pretraining setup or fit the original scaling-law functions.
record.method_sensitivity: Downstream task performance varies by task and model size; the Large model underperforms smaller models on several tasks, and average performance peaks at Base. The text also gives differing descriptions of the equal-FLOPs loss comparison.
record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 306, 2026
record.problems: The scaling range is limited to 25M–320M parameters. The reported scaling curves are not fitted to power laws, and the token-loss plots provide no numerical values in the text. The paper reports training loss rather than held-out loss. Its main text and Figure 22 description differ on which model has lower loss at equal FLOPs.

untested.parts: All parts: no language models, no held-out pretraining loss, no power-law fit.
All parts: no extrapolation from fits on small runs.
All parts: equal-FLOPs runs are compared, but the loss-minimising allocation is neither estimated nor fitted against compute.
All parts: shape is not varied at fixed parameter count.
Power-law functional form and exponents; held-out loss; other modalities and regimes beyond this behavioral-cloning setting.
Predictability of downstream performance from pretraining loss, beyond the equal-loss decision-action observation.

missing.what: Quantitative data-efficiency scaling: 10× more parameters yields roughly 3× better sample efficiency
Decision-action accuracy at equal training loss is higher for smaller models; motor actions show no size dependence
Placement precision @5px falls from 63.5% (Small) to 49.8% (Large), with drops on Animal Limb Tracking (40.9%→16.0%) and Multichannel Image Alignment (47.6%→16.9%)
Per-task autoregressive metrics across sizes: Large underperforms on Colored Dot, Multichannel and Road Network; ranges such as Cell Lineage 82–100% and Road Network 71–96%

record.verdict_notes: Training loss only; there is no held-out loss. Equal-FLOPs runs use training steps scaled by params × steps, and the Large model is trained for only 30K steps, so the Large model's weaker results may reflect undertraining. The authors are affiliated with an annotation company. Neither original source is this study.

versions.untested_parts: The models are behavioral-cloning models, not language models; the reported loss is training loss, not held-out pretraining loss.
No power laws fitted on small runs are used to predict the losses of much larger runs.
The study compares model sizes at approximately matched compute, but does not estimate the loss-minimising parameter/token allocation or fit its dependence on compute.
No comparison holds parameter count fixed while varying architecture details.

The study reports behavioral-cloning loss trends over 25M–320M parameters, but does not fit a power-law form or exponent. It does not test other modalities, repeated data, or whether the same law applies across other training regimes.
The study evaluates downstream task metrics across model sizes, but does not test predictability from pretraining loss.
No fitted exponents or systematic comparison of fitting choices is reported.

relationships.reason: Text: larger models are more data-efficient (10× params ≈ 3× sample efficiency), but no power law is fitted. Larger models also give no compute-efficiency gain at equal FLOPs (R5, R6), so the evidence is directional within a narrow range.
relationships.display_finding: A 10× parameter increase yielded approximately 3× greater sample efficiency but no efficiency gain at equal FLOPs, without a fitted power law.

relationships.condition: Autoregressive evaluation, average over 9 tasks, Base (95M) vs Large (320M)
relationships.reason: Average performance drops from 46.3% (Base) to 36.1% (Large), and two tasks stay below 2% at all sizes (R7–R10).
relationships.display_finding: Average performance across nine tasks fell from 46.3% at 95M to 36.1% at 320M, while two tasks remained below 2% at every size.

relationships.reason: Text: the average rises up to Base and then falls. Placement precision shows inverse scaling on some tasks. At equal loss, smaller models are better at decision actions. Improvement is non-monotonic and not predicted by loss. This is based on text not captured by the rows.
relationships.display_finding: Average performance rose through Base and then fell, placement precision declined with size on some tasks, and smaller models made better decisions at equal loss.
